summary: This RFC extends DKIM so a domain can ask for detailed reports when message authentication fails, and receivers can send them on demand. This helps domain owners find problems with signing or spoofing.

eli5.summary: If a signed letter fails the check, the receiver can send a note saying why, so the sender can fix problems.

questions: how to get dkim failure reports
what is the dkim r=y tag
what do dkim rr tokens mean
subtitle: How a domain can ask receivers to report back when its DKIM signatures fail to verify.

tldr.problem: A domain that signs its mail with DKIM has no standard way to learn when signatures that ought to verify are failing, or when unsigned mail violates its published signing practices.
tldr.mechanism: The signer adds an r=y tag to its DKIM-Signature and publishes a TXT record at _report._domainkey under its domain that holds a reporting address and parameters. A verifier whose check fails looks up that record and sends an ARF report.
tldr.outcome: Domains get failure reports without being able to direct them to outside addresses, but the record exposes them to floods of reports and the scheme cannot report fraudulent signatures lacking r=.

today: RFC 6651 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why DKIM Needs Failure Reports
sections.content:
DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) uses digital signatures to tie a domain name to a message. The verified domain can then be checked against sender policy, a known-good list or a reputation service. People deploying such technologies increasingly want to see DKIM verification failures and failures to follow published signing practices, such as Author Domain Signing Practices (ADSP).

RFC 6651 extends DKIM (RFC 6376) and ADSP (RFC 5617) with an optional reporting address and some reporting parameters. Reports use the format from RFC 6591, which builds on RFC 5965. The entity that sends reports is called a report generator: a DKIM Verifier that can also generate authentication failure reports.
sections.eli5: When a letter's secret seal looks wrong, the sender never hears about it. This gives the sender a way to ask to be told.

sections.title: The r= Tag and the Reporting Record
sections.content:
A Signer who wants failure reports adds one tag to its DKIM-Signature header field: r=, whose only legal value is y. It is optional and has no default.

The signer also publishes a DNS TXT record whose tag-value pairs look like DKIM key records but are independent of them and live at a different name. Unknown tags MUST be ignored. These tags are defined:

  • ra= is the reporting address, given as a local-part only. The verifier appends @ and the domain from the d= tag.
  • rp= is the requested report percentage, an integer from 0 to 100, defaulting to 100. Generators SHOULD NOT report more than this share of incidents.
  • rr= is a colon-separated list of the failure types to report, defaulting to all.
  • rs= is an SMTP error string the domain asks to have included if a message is rejected during the SMTP session.

Without an ra= tag, rp= and rr= MUST be ignored and no report may be issued.
sections.eli5: The sender puts a small sticker on each letter saying "tell me if this fails". Then it leaves a card at a known spot listing where to send the note and what kinds of problems it cares about.

sections.title: The Reporting Algorithm
sections.content:
For each DKIM-Signature that fails verification, a report generator MUST apply this algorithm or an equivalent. The DKIM evaluation outcome itself MUST NOT change.

  1. Stop if the field has no valid r= tag.
  2. Query DNS for a TXT record at _report._domainkey. followed by the d= domain, for example _report._domainkey.example.com.
  3. Stop if the response is not RCODE 0 (NOERROR) or if multiple TXT records come back.
  4. Join multiple strings as DKIM specifies, and stop if the content is syntactically invalid.
  5. Stop if the failure reason does not match rr=.
  6. If rp= is present, pick a random number from 0 to 99 and stop if it is not lower than the tag's value.
  7. Build the address from ra=, an @ and the d= domain, then send a report.
  8. If the SMTP session is still active and has not yet answered DATA, and rs= is present, the server SHOULD put the decoded string in its reply to DATA.

A generator SHOULD NOT send more than one report to any domain for a single message, and SHOULD cap the total reports one message can cause. The RFC points to three advantages. No extra DNS lookup is made until the signature fails. The DNS record confirms the request, so a malicious signer cannot claim that someone else wants reports. And reports cannot be steered to an address outside the signer's own domain.
sections.eli5: When a check fails, the receiver looks for the sticker, then for the card, then follows its instructions. It sends at most one note per sender per letter.

sections.title: ADSP Reporting and Report Types
sections.content:
The same four tags (ra, rp, rr, rs) are added to ADSP records, so a domain can learn when mail claiming to be from it arrives without a valid signature, contradicting its published practice. Here the address is built with the RFC5322.From domain of the message.

The rr= values name the failures wanted. Verifiers MUST NOT report incidents that do not match a request.

  • all: everything.
  • d: DNS problems such as key retrieval failures (DKIM only).
  • o: any other related reason.
  • p: rejection for local policy reasons.
  • s: signature or key syntax errors for DKIM; for ADSP, a valid signature that does not match the published policy.
  • u: unknown tags in the signature for DKIM; for ADSP, no valid signature and no match with policy.
  • v: verification failures or body hash mismatches (DKIM only).
  • x: signatures expired (DKIM only).

Reports MUST follow ARF and its authentication-failure extension, and generators are strongly advised to sign them with DKIM. Further guidance is in section 6 of RFC 6650.
sections.eli5: The sender can tick boxes for which problems it wants to hear about, such as an expired seal or a smudged one, and the receiver only reports those.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC's appendix shows a signature with the new tag, DKIM-Signature: v=1; a=rsa-sha256; c=simple/simple; d=example.com; s=jan2012; r=y; .... If the public key shows the signature invalid, the verifier queries _report._domainkey.example.com.

A sample TXT record there reads ra=dkim-errors; rp=100; rr=v:x. It asks for reports at the address dkim-errors at the signer's domain, for all incidents (100%), and only for verification failures and expired signatures. An ADSP example is dkim=all; ra=dkim-adsp-errors; rr=u.
sections.eli5: An example: example.com leaves a card saying "write to dkim-errors, tell me every time, but only about broken or old seals".

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Volume is unpredictable, so implementers should expect substantial traffic.

The main risk is deliberate misuse. Publishing the reporting record makes a domain a target: an attacker can add r=y to existing signatures, add a bogus signature, or craft a whole new message with r=y and a d= pointing at the victim. A spam run of millions of messages with a fake d=example.com; r=y signature would make receivers report failures to example.com in the millions and in short order. Implementers are strongly advised to publish the record only when reports are desired.

Negative caching offers some protection, but only for the negative time-to-live on the SOA record. Positive caching means removing the record does not stop reports immediately, so a low TTL should be considered.

Fraudulent signatures that carry no r= tag are never reported. Looking for the record without r= would create a denial-of-service attack, so this gap is accepted.
sections.eli5: If you tell everyone where to send complaints, a prankster can fake lots of bad letters to flood you. So only turn this on when you really want the notes.
